claims.text: The initially solid particles are as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with native, unmodified surface chemistry.
Surface segregation of Cu triggers the onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Cu segregation produces a Cu-rich, liquid-like surface layer below the bulk melting point.
The Cu-rich surface layer acts as a nucleation zone from which melting propagates into the particle core.
Cu is a lower-melting constituent relative to the other components relevant to the proposed segregation mechanism.
On heating, Cu preferentially diffuses to and enriches the nanoparticle surface.
The Cu-rich liquid-like layer lowers the local melting temperature at the particle exterior.
Melting proceeds from the surface into the interior rather than as a homogeneous phase transition.
Native-surface nanoparticles will begin surface premelting at a lower temperature than passivated nanoparticles.
Native nanoparticles will form a thin Cu-rich liquid layer at temperatures significantly below their measured bulk melting point.
The thickness of the surface liquid layer will evolve measurably with increasing temperature.
Surface effects relevant to the proposed mechanism are pronounced for high-surface-to-volume-ratio nanoparticles, typically smaller than 100 nm.
An inert atmosphere or vacuum minimizes oxidation and external chemical reactions during heating.
Particle size, synthesis history, and local defect structure may affect the temperatures at which segregation and premelting begin.
Surface oxidation or other compositional gradients may alter the proposed melting mechanism.
Failure to observe either a native-versus-passivated difference in premelting or Cu enrichment associated with premelting would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as nanoparticles with native, unmodified surfaces, but the predicted outcome also describes a lower premelting onset in native samples relative to the baseline. Native samples cannot be lower than an identically defined native baseline; the intended comparator appears to be the passivated group.
